claims.claim_text: By the early 2010s roughly a dozen companies had passed one million dollars a year in revenue selling open-source hobbyist boards and kits, with SparkFun above ten million dollars a year and Adafruit near one million from a two-person operation.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's about a dozen companies that have broken this million dollar mark
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Before standard open-source licences existed, an engineer wanting to publish a design on defined terms had to write the terms themselves or pay a lawyer several thousand dollars to draft them; off-the-shelf licences replaced that cost with a choice among pre-drafted, court-defensible instruments.
claims.quote_verbatim: you had to go and pay some lawyer $5,000 or something to do that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cultural Differences

claims.claim_text: The open source hardware definition requires a licence that permits commercial use: attribution and share-alike terms qualify, while the non-commercial variant of Creative Commons does not, so a design released with a non-commercial clause cannot be called open source hardware even though every design file is public.
claims.quote_verbatim: it must not be the non-commercial version. It must only be the attribute only
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: A non-commercial licence publishes the same information as a permissive one; the difference is only that the copyright holder reserves the right to sell the product, so the internals are documented but a competing manufacture is barred.
claims.quote_verbatim: the information's exactly the same. It's open, but, uh, you are not, but nobody is allowed, nobody, but you, the copyright holder is allowed to make money from it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: For a product released as open source hardware the only exclusive right left to the originator is the trademark on the product name; the PCB, schematic and everything else may be copied lawfully.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only way I can protect it is to, um, or, or you, if you're making your open hardware product is to trademark the name and then they're not allowed to use the name, but they can copy your PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: A patent discloses the invention but not the files needed to build it, whereas an open source hardware release hands over the PCB file, the schematic and the bill of materials, that is, the complete manufacturing package.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't actually give away all of your actual, uh, files to manufacture it, you know, whereas an open source, you'll give it away your PCB file, your schematic, your bill of materials
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: Publication is a defensive strategy against later patents: an idea that is published enters the prior-art record, so anyone who subsequently files on the same idea can be challenged.
claims.quote_verbatim: the best defense for the future is to publish everything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and Self Publishing

claims.claim_text: In the early open hardware period the de facto schematic and layout package was Eagle, which was free at entry level but proprietary with a closed file format; the only fully open EDA alternatives were gEDA and KiCad.
claims.quote_verbatim: de facto standard EDA package in the open source hardware industry is Eagle. That's right. Because it's free, but it's not open source. It's closed. It's freemium
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Dave Is Back And Blogging!

claims.claim_text: One position on tooling purity holds that a design is not truly open unless it can be edited with open tools, but a documented, open file format is a workable substitute because it lets the design cross into other tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: The, the file format is closed and DJ made the concession that maybe if the file format was open, that would be enough
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Dave Is Back And Blogging!

claims.claim_text: Eagle's free tier restricted board size and layer count, and lifting those limits required the paid version at roughly six to eight hundred dollars, which meant a released design could exceed what a recipient could legally open.
claims.quote_verbatim: Anyway, you can buy the full version for like $600, $800 or something
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Dave Is Back And Blogging!

claims.claim_text: Publishing complete construction articles in hobbyist electronics magazines was the pre-Internet form of open hardware; what the open source hardware movement added was not the practice of publishing but a formal licensing framework around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's only new from a point of view that, you know, they started up this license, you know, thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality

claims.claim_text: An Arduino board is a costly, high-level platform relative to the circuitry a task needs; where size, weight or unit cost matter, as on a quadcopter, the appropriate step is to lay a custom board carrying only the required circuitry.
claims.quote_verbatim: because the Arduino is an expensive, high-level platform. It's great for the beginner
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Hard Work Hypothesis

claims.claim_text: A common failure mode of open hardware releases is face-value openness: the files are posted once when the board ships and then neither maintained nor supported, leaving the design effectively abandoned.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's kind of face value open source, right? Oh, this is open. Here's our files. And then it's left to dead
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Hard Work Hypothesis

claims.claim_text: Sustained supply of an open hardware product requires an organisation with full-time staff and working capital; the widely used open platforms are produced by companies rather than by individuals working evenings.
claims.quote_verbatim: it needs these companies with the resources and the money and the full-time and people who are working on it full-time to produce and actually supply to the market these open source hardware products
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Hard Work Hypothesis

claims.claim_text: The overwhelming majority of users of an open hardware product buy the finished, supported board and never open the design files, so a project only reaches wide use when someone manufactures and supports a polished product at a good price. Openness alone does not achieve this.
claims.quote_verbatim: 90 plus percent of people who use open source, who make open source products, open source hardware products popular, use the finished product
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Hard Work Hypothesis

claims.claim_text: Nothing in an open hardware licence prevents a third party from sending the published files to a contract manufacturer and undercutting the originator; the constraint on this behaviour is commercial and social rather than legal.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could come along and make an Arduino board tomorrow, get it manufactured in China and undercut the Arduino team and put them out of business probably
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Ben & Jeri Show

claims.claim_text: Schematics have been released under the GPL, but its enforceability against hardware is untested; the open source hardware licence was drafted specifically to cover hardware-specific matters that a software licence does not address.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the only one out there, the only license out there that includes hardware-specific things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: The advantage of using an established hardware licence over improvising is that the text has been reviewed by lawyers for suitability to hardware, which an engineer picking terms on intuition cannot verify.
claims.quote_verbatim: the open-source hardware license has been vetted by, you know, smart lawyer geeks to be suitable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Creative Commons exists in several variants and the choice among them is the licensor's, but to qualify under the open source hardware definition the chosen terms must permit commercial reproduction of the design by others.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, the open-source hardware is... You have to allow commercial reproduction as well
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: The working norm in open hardware distinguishes derivation from duplication: producing a modified or improved version is expected and unobjectionable, while taking the files unchanged, contributing nothing back and displacing the originator is legal but treated as a breach of custom.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if they just directly take your files and make no changes, give nothing back to the community, and just put you out of business, then that's frowned upon
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Practical enforcement against unlicensed copies usually runs through the marketplace rather than the copier: the originator asks the retailer or platform to stop carrying items that violate the licence terms.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can try to get them not to carry things that violate the Creative Commons or open source hardware license
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Exhilarating ESC Escapades

claims.claim_text: Litigation is not an available remedy at the scale of most open hardware: the value of a small kit is far below the cost of pursuing an infringer, so licence terms operate mainly as a statement of expectation.
claims.quote_verbatim: What are you going to do? Sue them over a little breadboard kit?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Exhilarating ESC Escapades

claims.claim_text: An unattributed clone imposes a hidden support cost on the original designer, because buyers of the copy bring their problems to the original project's support forum; the designer's defence is to state publicly that unsold units are not supported.
claims.quote_verbatim: she was having to support people that didn't even buy their kits from her
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Exhilarating ESC Escapades

claims.claim_text: Attribution is the cheapest obligation in an open hardware licence: copying and selling the design is permitted outright, and the only requirement is a credit line, which costs the copier nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're allowed to copy it and sell it. So why you wouldn't just do a simple thing like putting a credit on your webpage or something is beyond me
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Exhilarating ESC Escapades

claims.claim_text: Arduino's commercial position rests on trademark rather than design exclusivity: clones of the board are lawful, but only the company may use the name, so a compatible board must be identifiable as not being a genuine unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arduino distinguishes itself by saying, you know, only we can use our trademark and our name
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: For a small board of twenty or thirty parts the native design file format matters little in practice, because anyone wanting to rebuild it can re-lay the design from the schematic in a few hours; the format argument bites hardest on large designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: does it actually matter if the files are in Altium format? Probably not
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: Open hardware has produced nothing on the collaborative scale of the Linux kernel, because a single circuit board does not partition among contributors: past three or four designers on one board the work splinters rather than accumulating.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think that hardware is as capable of doing something that big because if it's a single board, you get more than three or four designers on it and it's just going to splinter
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: The open source hardware definition came first and carried no licence of its own; until a dedicated instrument was published, projects had to borrow software licences such as the GPL.
claims.quote_verbatim: Open source had an open source hardware definition, but it didn't actually come with a license
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Vafrous Video Vaniloquence

claims.claim_text: The CERN open hardware licence took the existing open hardware definition and turned it into a lawyer-reviewed legal framework, which is the difference between a statement of principles and terms intended to be enforceable.
claims.quote_verbatim: And now I think the difference is it's a legal framework now. So now it's like enforceable. They had lawyers look all this over
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Vafrous Video Vaniloquence

claims.claim_text: A recurring form of open-source washing is a product advertised as open hardware whose published schematic and silkscreen carry a company copyright notice and whose PCB and CAD files are not actually downloadable.
claims.quote_verbatim: Since when do you put copyright on an open source product, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shonky Stiver Stultiloquence

claims.claim_text: Releasing only the firmware or software does not make a product open source hardware; the hardware release must include the PCB and schematic files, and the bill of materials, on the principle of giving away as much information as possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: open source hardware is a very, very specific thing. You must give away your PCB and schematic files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shonky Stiver Stultiloquence

claims.claim_text: Open hardware transparency stops at the design: profit margins, volumes, supplier identities, accounting, web-store operation and shipping arrangements stay private, because a business cannot function with those exposed.
claims.quote_verbatim: there do have to be some limits to the transparency for you to remain a business, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: Very few open hardware licences have been tested in court, and the typical developer of an open hardware product has neither the money nor the inclination to engage lawyers, so the licence functions in practice as a declared expectation rather than an enforced contract.
claims.quote_verbatim: And very few of them have actually been tested in the legal system
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: Because the standard open hardware licences carry no non-commercial clause, a large company need not acquire a small open hardware company to obtain its work; it can take the published designs directly and manufacture them at its own scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could just pick and choose from the open hardware designs
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: A BeagleBoard successor moved its BGA packages from 0.4 mm to 0.8 mm ball pitch specifically so that users could fabricate their own boards: finer pitch tightens solder-mask and etch tolerances and raises board cost, which defeats the purpose of publishing the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Your boards are more expensive to manufacture because the tolerances are all tighter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: A slowdown in Moore's law favours open hardware because shared mechanical platforms only repay their design cost when interfaces are stable; while heatsinks, sockets and form factors change every year or two, an open laptop chassis cannot amortise.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'd be crazy to sort of build an open laptop chassis because every two years or one year, the heat sinks change and the socket formats change
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Hardware's natural protection is the six to twelve months a competitor needs to develop an equivalent product; publishing the design files removes that lead time entirely, leaving only an unwritten rule against competing directly with the originator.
claims.quote_verbatim: Anyone can take your files and go and compete directly against you. They shouldn't because that's one of the unwritten rules of open source hardware is you don't do that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Licence terms are sometimes changed to satisfy a funder rather than for engineering reasons: one instrument company moved to a non-commercial licence while negotiating funding to place its devices in schools.
claims.quote_verbatim: we changed it when we were talking to people who wanted to give us money to put our devices in schools
claims.speaker: Ian Daniher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: A product has more layers than its circuit board, and competitive advantage can be held in firmware and host software even when the hardware is fully published, so the whole stack need not be locked down to keep a defensible position.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's really how you do it in open source hardware, I think, is that you have more layers in terms of firmware, in terms of software
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Hardware has roughly seven layers where software has one: schematic, board layout, bill of materials, assembly instructions, documentation and mechanical CAD, each needing its own collaboration mechanism, licence answer and preferred file format. Version control tools that diff ASCII cleanly cannot show a meaningful difference between two board files.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very hard for them to show you a diff on a pretty circuit board file
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: For a commodity board built from published Eagle files, the observed interval between product release and a competing clone reaching the market was under seven days, which is why some designers withhold their native design files.
claims.quote_verbatim: it now takes less than seven days for the Chinese to clone us and basically put a clone of our product into the marketplace
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Selling hardware while the accompanying software is written and given away by volunteers creates a support mismatch: buyers who paid for the board treat the vendor as responsible for software defects and documentation they did not pay for and the vendor did not write.
claims.quote_verbatim: the software is created by a community of volunteers and given away for free
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Linux was released without warranty and with thin documentation, which created the opening for paid third-party support businesses; the same gap exists around open hardware, where a vendor is well advised either to supply software support or to sell it as an option.
claims.quote_verbatim: That was a market opportunity for companies like Red Hat and IBM to provide third-party services
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The Tangibot crowdfunding campaign proposed to take the MakerBot design unchanged to a Chinese manufacturer under a different name, adding no modification, and was legally entitled to do so under the open source licence; the campaign did not reach its funding target.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to take the MakerBot to China as is and I'm going to call it the Tangibot. And, you know, I am allowed to do this because it's open source hardware
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Entering medium-volume hardware typically requires two to ten million dollars of capital, which normally comes from venture investors who expect protectable intellectual property, so openness and the funding route needed to reach that volume pull against each other.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need anywhere from, you know, two to probably more like 10 million of funding
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: No rule in the open source hardware definition dictates when files must be released. Publishing design files before you have manufactured and put the product on sale invites someone else to produce it first, so the usual practice is to release at or after launch.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can call it open hardware and then once you're manufacturing and got it on sale, then you can release the design files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: MakerBot was founded on a fully open 3D printer and later closed part of the design of the Replicator 2; the company was venture-capital funded, and its obligation to return capital is the mechanism behind that change.
claims.quote_verbatim: MakerBot is in this to make money, right? They're venture capital funded
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: The engineering case for the early open MakerBot is that its first iterations were poor at repeatability and usability, and outside contributors working on the open platform improved the build platform and software that the company had shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of very resourceful hackers came together and, like, started glomming things onto it and improving the build platform
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Clone economics played out concretely on the MakerBot design: a Chinese company took the original files, made cosmetic changes and sold the printer more cheaply than the originator, well before any comparable domestic effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've basically taken the original files, tweaked them a bit, made it look a little bit different, and you can buy one fairly cheaply
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: For a complex product the practical value of openness is the ability to modify, not the ability to build from scratch: an individual sourcing every part in unit quantities pays prices that make self-building uneconomic, and the assembly and bring-up work is substantial.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sourcing everything in small volumes is a, your prices, your costs would go through the roof
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Creative Commons licences are a poor fit for hardware because a physical design is not fully covered by copyright and raises patent questions as well; the TAPR open hardware licence and the later CERN open hardware licence were written to address hardware specifically.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't just really cover it by copyright and there are patent issues and all sorts of other things
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: On the strict reading, any licence carrying a non-commercial flag is not open, because openness is defined by what the recipient may do with the result rather than by how much information was published.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I see any license that has a non-commercial flag on it as being non-open because it's restricted what people can do with the end result
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Creative Commons attribution share-alike imposes two obligations on a recipient of a hardware design: credit the originator, and release derivative work under the same terms.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the past, we've done a lot of Creative Commons attribution share alike. So you have to share it as well and you have to put our name on it
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: One open hardware design house moved from attribution share-alike to public domain release, reserving only the trademark on the product name, on the reasoning that development and breakout boards exist to be built on and licence conditions on them are friction with no purpose.
claims.quote_verbatim: We just claim all rights except our trademark on the name
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers oriented to open hardware will take runs far below conventional minimums, in the tens of units, which is what allows an untested design to be offered for sale without the designer carrying inventory risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: We can make as few as 20 and try to sell them
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A viable division of labour for a small open hardware operation is to keep design, documentation, firmware and user support in-house and to farm out manufacturing, fulfilment and distribution to a partner willing to run batches of one hundred to one thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: to have someone supporting open hardware with batches of 100 to 500 to 1,000 is just really excellent
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Many designs are worth building but not worth productising: where the return does not justify the production and ongoing support burden, the design can be released as public domain and the bare boards distributed at cost so others can build it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we decide ultimately that the cost-benefit ratio of getting it into production versus supporting it and what we're going to make on it in the end just isn't worth it
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: MakerBot, after several years and venture funding, concluded it could not continue as a fully open company and closed parts of its design in order to grow; that outcome is the standing counterexample cited against fully open hardware businesses at scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: we cannot continue as a 100% pure open source hardware company. We have to close several aspects of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Cloud-hosted part-library tools default to publishing the symbols and footprints a user creates, so an organisation adopting one must decide in advance how much its footprint and symbol work discloses about the parts it designs with.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of our, our, our default policy is that, um, that pretty much everything is public, right?
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: A workable split for an open hardware release is two bills of materials: a public one carrying descriptions and manufacturer part numbers, and a private one carrying vendors, negotiated prices and qualified alternates. The sourcing work in the second represents most of the effort and is the part that is withheld.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got a version of the bomb which I release to the public
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: Raspberry Pi initially released schematics but not Gerbers, drawing the line where disclosure would have compromised the negotiated component pricing that its vendor relationships depended on.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually drew the line based on, you know, trying to maintain vendor relationships because they're getting, you know, upfront pricing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: MakerBot had sold about twenty-two thousand printers in its four-year history at low margin when Stratasys acquired it for roughly four hundred million dollars in stock, so the price cannot be explained by the financial performance of the business.
claims.quote_verbatim: in their whole four-year history, right, they've only sold 22,000 printers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Because most of MakerBot's technology was published, the acquisition could not have been for the technology: what was bought was the brand and the community around it, the assets that openness does not transfer to a copier.
claims.quote_verbatim: they didn't buy them for the technology, right? Because most of it is open
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Forking a hardware design is straightforward but reintegration is not: changes made to a PCB in a derivative cannot be merged back into the parent the way a code branch can, so hardware forks tend to diverge permanently.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, you can't do it at the PCB level, you know?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Arduino, IndiGoGo and Hack-a-Day - Doodad Dealer Dancing

claims.claim_text: A development-tool vendor selling open hardware can move from idea to shipped board quickly because one engineer carries a project end to end, paperwork is minimal, and development boards of this kind do not require FCC testing.
claims.quote_verbatim: a project is usually, uh, worked on by one engineer as opposed to a team of people
claims.speaker: Chris Taylor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: IBM published the PC expansion bus and the BIOS listing while retaining copyright on the BIOS, which let third parties build cards and machines around it; that published bus became the ISA standard, following the earlier Altair and S-100 buses.
claims.quote_verbatim: they came and they opened the bus and everything else they published the bias listing
claims.episode_title: Hyperloop, Upverter and Soldering - Unbelievable USB Ustulater

claims.claim_text: Ubertooth One needed four layers, which exceeded the free tier of Eagle; rather than buy an upgrade the designer moved to KiCad, on the reasoning that an open design is not usable if modifying it requires the recipient to buy a proprietary licence.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't want people to have to pay for a license for some software to modify my open source design
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The Daisho architecture is a mainboard carrying an FPGA, RAM and a USB 3.0 link to a host, with pluggable front-end boards each holding the connectors and PHY transceivers for one high-speed medium such as USB 3.0, gigabit Ethernet or HDMI. Signals pass in through one transceiver, through the FPGA and out the other, giving a man-in-the-middle path for monitoring, injection and on-the-fly modification.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a main board that has an FPGA and some RAM and a USB 3.0 backend to a, to a host computer. And then there are pluggable front end boards
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Running an open hardware project with the apparatus of open source software, public repositories, wikis, mailing lists and IRC channels, converts users into contributors; one such project recruited its entire contractor pool from volunteers who had already done good work on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the things that people commonly do to execute and support open source software projects, I do with my open source hardware projects
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A kit maker deliberately kept its firmware within the code-size limits of the free PIC compiler, using all but the last four words of memory rather than buying the several-hundred-dollar optimising compiler, because a paid compiler would have made the published firmware unbuildable by its users.
claims.quote_verbatim: then the problem is that other people wouldn't be able to re recompile the firmware without paying that few hundred dollars
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: 3D printing production enclosures does not scale: a crowdfunded product that printed its own cases ended up running a room of printers continuously, and the designer identified it afterwards as a mistake against injection moulding.
claims.quote_verbatim: They had to have, you know, a room full of 3D printers just running 24-7
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: HackRF was funded under DARPA's Cyber Fast Track programme on an explicit proposal to prototype a software-defined radio, build five hundred units, give them away and publish everything the project produced as open source.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd like to build 500 of them and give them away for free. And I would like it to entirely be open source and publish absolutely everything produced by this project
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: In the absence of enforceable exclusivity, reputation is the operative sanction in open hardware trade: a company that clones a competitor's published design outright loses standing with the customers and suppliers it shares with the originator.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's how the open source hardware industry works. It works on your reputation
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: There is no legal mechanism in the United States for placing a work into the public domain by declaration; a designer intending that result must instead apply the most permissive licence available, which is why nominally public-domain hardware releases carry licence text.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no law that allows you to make something public domain. The only thing you can do is apply the most permissive license you can possibly find
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: A patent is already a public disclosure, so a patent pledge changes nothing about what can be read; what it changes is enforcement, amounting to a commitment by the holder not to sue those who practise the invention.
claims.quote_verbatim: they said that they're going to open source all their patents and, you know, basically release them into the public domain as much as they can
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: Taking venture funding transfers the decision on whether a product stays open away from the founder; the remaining choices are to accept the direction or to leave, which is the usual mechanism behind an open product being closed.
claims.quote_verbatim: They took, you know, venture capital funding and things like that. And once you do that, you don't make the decisions anymore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Replicability constrains design freedom in an open project: parts should ideally be chosen from a shared, obtainable base set, because a design built entirely from custom-specified parts cannot be reproduced by anyone else even when every file is published.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go down that road too far and you do everything custom, then if it's an open source project, how is anyone supposed to replicate what you did?
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Extensibility in hardware depends on component availability rather than on file access: users can only build on a published design if they can buy the parts it uses, which is a structural difference from open source software.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can't buy things that you're able to incorporate into your projects, then you also can't really extend them
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Openness in hardware is a sliding scale rather than a binary property, and the practical question is where a release sits on it: a design authored in a tool the recipient cannot open is a hindrance regardless of what licence is attached.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's always going to be a sliding scale
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: A workable practical test for openness is whether one other person in the world could build what you built: if they would need a supply agreement with a chip vendor, or a paid EDA licence to open the files, the design fails the test.
claims.quote_verbatim: can one person in the world build what you built?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: The Raspberry Pi does not meet the open source hardware definition, because reproducing it would require a relationship with Broadcom for the application processor that an individual cannot obtain.
claims.quote_verbatim: even the Raspberry Pi is not open source hardware, right? You know, like having to deal with Broadcom
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: An open instrument design serves two distinct downstream uses: add-on hardware built on top of the platform, such as the PortaPack for HackRF, and wholesale reuse of parts of the design inside another product, the second of which is only possible because the files are published.
claims.quote_verbatim: others may be people taking the HackRF design and, you know, taking parts of it or all of it and incorporating it into another electronic design. And they can do that because it's open source
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Asked what protects an open source hardware product against being copied, practitioners in the field have consistently named one mechanism only: the trademark. That is the whole of the legal position, which is why trademark disputes are existential for such companies.
claims.quote_verbatim: literally the only thing they said was their protection was trademark
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: An exclusive manufacturing agreement is a structural hazard for an open hardware company: with such an agreement in place the design owner cannot move production elsewhere when the relationship breaks down, even though the design itself is public.
claims.quote_verbatim: they claim to have an exclusive agreement with the Arduino company, right, for exclusive manufacture of Arduino boards
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: Open hardware cannot be run on donated effort alone in the way an open software project can, because boards must be purchased before they can be sold; the physical goods require working capital regardless of how the design work is funded.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to purchase boards, you need actual capital
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: Permitting others to manufacture a published design while withholding the originator's name and logo serves a practical purpose beyond branding: it stops buyers of third-party units from arriving at the original designer for support of hardware they did not build.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want people coming to me for support for something that you've manufactured
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: The WildFire sensor board published as open hardware carried an ATmega1284P with 128 KB of flash and 16 KB of RAM, a CC3000 Wi-Fi module, an SD card and an external watchdog timer, replacing an ATmega328-class node that had proved short of resources.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got like 128 K of flash and 16 K of Ram
claims.speaker: Vic Aprea
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: Openness can be used as leverage in component negotiation: because the published board acts as a public reference design for every chip on it, silicon vendors accepted pricing they would not have offered for an equivalent closed product, which was what made a ninety-nine dollar target reachable.
claims.quote_verbatim: open source helped a huge amount because it became a kind of reference design for a lot of these chips on the board
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Injection-moulded enclosure CAD is the layer manufacturers withhold most readily, and with reason: the value is in the fifty thousand dollars of tooling rather than in the geometry, and no user is going to have moulds cut to modify the case.
claims.quote_verbatim: Nobody's going to go out there and get, you know, $50,000 molds made and, you know, and remake this thing and tweak it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Be Tidy

claims.claim_text: Neither the term open source hardware nor the original gear logo is legally controlled, so a product that fails the definition can still carry both; the certification mark introduced later is the only element with enforceable control over its use.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's nothing stopping me from using either the name open source hardware or using the open gear logo
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Be Tidy

claims.claim_text: Open source EDA projects are positioned to try designs the commercial vendors cannot, because a venture-backed tool company aiming to be acquired must imitate the incumbents to be an attractive target; the open project has no such constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: open source is not enough. You need to innovate
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: Comparing a Raspberry Pi with an Allwinner-based competitor turns on component availability rather than licence text: the Broadcom part cannot be bought by a third party at all, while the competing board's silicon can be, which is what makes one design reproducible and the other not.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't buy those chips, whereas the other one you can. And it is open source
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: Crowd Supply operates as a curated product launch platform for open hardware in which crowdfunding is only the first stage: it also handles fulfilment, marketing and continued sale of stock after delivery, and about ninety per cent of the products it carries are open in some form.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd say 90% of what we do is open in some way or another
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: OpenRex was designed as a fully open board, open for commercial use as well, combining a microcontroller for real-time work with an applications processor for a graphical Linux environment, on the reasoning that existing single-board computers were blocked from full openness by closed processor documentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: even Raspberry Pi, it's not really open source. I think the Broadcom chip, there is some closed documentation
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: The open source hardware gear logo carries no information about how open a product actually is, because it is applied by anyone who releases anything, from a full file set down to a schematic PDF; a viewer cannot tell from the mark what has been released.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's being used by everyone, regardless of how open their product is
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: One proposed remedy for the ambiguity of the gear logo is to append Creative-Commons-style letters indicating which layers have been released, so that a viewer can see at a glance whether the schematic, PCB, firmware and mechanical CAD are open and whether the licence carries a non-commercial clause. The Open Source Hardware Association instead introduced a separately trademarked certification mark under its own control.
claims.quote_verbatim: I proposed a change to the open source hardware logo. So it had the letters telling you what parts are open
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: One workable practice for a vendor with a mixed product line is to apply the gear logo only to the fully open, commercially licensed board and to leave it off the module released for non-commercial use.
claims.quote_verbatim: We only use the gear logo on the fully open board
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: An established instrument manufacturer can often be persuaded to open a schematic and some or all of the firmware, but not the mechanical CAD, because releasing the case files together with the bill of materials would let a competitor reproduce the whole product.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think I'm ever going to be able to convince them to open all the mechanical CAD files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: An open hardware product can be monetised for a window long enough to fund the next design even without patent or copyright protection, provided the business is structured to end rather than to be defended indefinitely; the absence of a monopoly forces the designer to keep moving.
claims.quote_verbatim: even without sort of really strong patent or copyright protection, I'm able to sort of monetize my ideas for a period of time. That's long enough for me to get to the next generation
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Splitting a design task between two people is slower than leaving it with one, because interface overhead exceeds the gain; the crossover where division starts to pay is around five engineers of comparable ability, which is the team size at which products no individual could design become possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: the point at which you start amortizing, splitting a project is around five
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Distributed hardware collaboration is bounded by physical shipping rather than by tooling: a change committed to a software repository is visible to a collaborator in seconds, whereas a hardware revision must be prototyped, shipped and re-instrumented, giving iteration cycles measured in weeks. Each collaborator also needs an equipped bench and comparable assembly skill.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I make a change to something in the hardware, I have to FedEx it to you
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Altium implemented multi-user concurrent PCB co-design, which is difficult to build and was largely unused, indicating that the constraint on collaborative board design is how the work partitions rather than whether the tool permits simultaneous editing.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think anyone actually uses that feature
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: A hardware implant is a malicious device installed on a system to grant software privilege and then withdraw; before the leaked intelligence catalogues of 2013, public knowledge of the category extended little further than games-console mod chips, and the NSA Playset reimplemented catalogue devices cheaply using open source hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: These are reimaginations or similar devices to what the catalog had, but we're going to do them with open source hardware and do them cheap
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe FitzPatrick

claims.claim_text: Building a product around a single-board computer that is not open makes the business wholly dependent on that board's continued manufacture: if the vendor discontinues the version, the only options are to port the application or to stop selling.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're totally reliant upon the continued manufacturer of that board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Paparazzi UAV, begun in 2003 at ENAC in France, is the origin point of the open-source UAV autopilot lineage from which later open autopilot electronics descend.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's pretty much the grandfather of all open source UAV autopilot systems
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Publishing a development board's KiCad design files and its footprint alongside them gives a direct path from prototype to product: the working sub-circuit can be pasted into the user's own board rather than reimplemented, and the module itself can be placed in a design too small for a vendor discovery board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the design files in key cut are in the repository. So if you prototype something with the one bitsy, uh, at the end, you can just copy and paste the design into your thing that you're making
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The reverse engineering of an FPGA bitstream format and the open toolchain built on it were done largely in spare time by a handful of people with limited resources, which implies that a well-resourced organisation could do the same to any undocumented bitstream. Documenting the format would remove the incentive.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a very, very small group of people, um, with, uh, very limited resources. Um, and it was not that hard actually
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: The recurring waste in hardware is redesign from scratch, or private modification of a working design with no change flowing back, so the original never improves; publishing designs and firmware at least removes the non-recurring engineering from the next board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the amount of time people like start from scratch or take something that used to work and change it slightly, but never contribute back to the original thing
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: A published project should state the constraints behind its bill of materials cost, because a newcomer comparing their own six-hundred-dollar BOM against an undisclosed one has no way to see which constraints, subsidies or volumes produced the difference.
claims.quote_verbatim: I always kind of push back on projects that hide the cost
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: A large archive of open projects addressing the same problem is usable as engineering evidence: it shows which sensors recur, which circuits around them work, why those choices were made, and where the same dead ends are being hit repeatedly.
claims.quote_verbatim: are there certain sensors that are really popular? Are there certain circuits designed around those that work really well? Why are those choices being made?
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: The buildlog.net 2.x laser was an early comprehensive open-source laser cutter, developed and documented publicly at a time when a commercial machine cost eighteen to twenty thousand dollars, and roughly four hundred kits were sold from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was really the first comprehensive open source laser
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Eagle held the low-end EDA position for years because the open hardware movement standardised on it, which is also where its support material accumulated; KiCad displaced it from that position once it reached comparable capability without a subscription.
claims.quote_verbatim: Eagle's being the de facto standard low end for a long time now, just because the open source hardware movement started using that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motivational Speaker

claims.claim_text: Open hardware in the biomedical domain runs into regulation rather than licensing: making or implying a diagnostic claim about a device brings it within a regulatory approval regime, so open instruments in this area must be framed and scoped to avoid diagnostic claims.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't mention anything diagnostic or say anything diagnostic. Uh-huh. As that also means that you should have regulatory approval
claims.speaker: Jean Rintoul
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jean Rintoul

claims.claim_text: Keeping open boards deliberately simple, on the order of twenty to twenty-five components, serves the commercial user as well as the beginner: a simple published design can be lifted into the customer's own product or adjusted and manufactured by them, which a complex one cannot.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything we do is open source. So they, uh, if they're more commercial using, they might want to actually take that design and then integrate it into something they're designing
claims.speaker: Ken Burns
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: The practical attraction of an open instruction set architecture such as RISC-V to an implementer is the absence of licensing exposure: an openly given specification removes the risk of litigation that accompanies implementing a proprietary ISA.
claims.quote_verbatim: because everything is open and just given away for free, I don't have to worry about like in a can of lawyers ending up at my front door
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: The DIN SPEC documents give open source hardware a formal standards footing: one part sets out an operational definition broken into objective criteria for judging whether a piece of hardware complies, and the other defines a community-based certification procedure against it.
claims.quote_verbatim: DIN spec 3501-2 defines requirements for implementing a community-based certification procedure for open source hardware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Published open hardware clusters around comparatively simple designs, historically around ATmega328-class boards; the most technically interesting hardware is generally not released, which limits what the open corpus can teach beyond the introductory level.
claims.quote_verbatim: the most interesting stuff is just not going to be open sourced
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Working in open silicon requires inverting conventional ASIC practice: release early, publish openly and describe the design publicly before it has been taped out, because the aim is to seed an ecosystem in which designs build on one another.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should flip all your assumptions about how you should do something. Uh, you should release it early. You should publish it openly
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The common objection to publishing a design is that giving away the work removes the chance to be paid for it; the counter-argument from practice is that the published work is what brings the next piece of work, since the field has far more problems than practitioners.
claims.quote_verbatim: more likely you will actually bring notoriety to yourself and you'll be asked to do the next interesting thing
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A process design kit is foundry intellectual property, so the first compromise for open chip design was to host open tools and an obfuscated foundry PDK together in the cloud: usable through the portal but not downloadable, since downloading implies full exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: we put the open source solution on the cloud and we put the foundry PDK on the cloud as well, but obfuscated
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Once a PDK is genuinely open rather than merely hosted, the whole flow can be built and run locally from public repositories, which allows far more iteration; the first openly available nodes were 130 nm at GlobalFoundries, 180 nm at another fab, and 130 nm from SkyWater.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use 130 nanometer on global foundries or 180 nanometer next fab
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Open tools plus sponsored shuttle runs remove the funding gate that used to sit before a chip existed: a designer can carry an idea to finished silicon first and then approach investors with a completed pre-silicon result rather than a slide deck and a track record.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if I want to go to the investor, I can actually say that I have this. I've developed it. I have a pre-silicon
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Publishing tested carrier boards for a system-on-module is a support strategy as much as a licensing one: a customer respins a validated baseboard into their own form factor and reuses its circuitry, so long as the module interface is reproduced correctly.
claims.quote_verbatim: use one of those baseboards as a template and slap our SOM on there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: For a consultant, publishing a design around a new interface or capability functions as verifiable proof of competence and generates referrals from the platform vendor, who has more integration requests than capacity to serve them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you publish some designs, usually that's a great way to get your name out and like show that you can interface to this thing
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: An open IP effort has to cover two pillars at once, the blocks themselves and the tools and workflows used to build with them, because an open core is unusable to anyone who cannot afford the half-million-dollar tool licence needed to work with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want an open source IP core that then nobody can use because they can't pay half a million dollar license to work with it
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: The recurring open hardware question is not whether to publish but how far down the stack to go: a PDF schematic, the native schematic and PCB files, the bill of materials, supplier information, or a full turnkey package that lets anyone manufacture the product without further work.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like, well, how much do you give away? Is a PDF schematic enough?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware Update Capabilities

claims.claim_text: A substantial amount of internal silicon and verification tooling at large semiconductor companies could be released without commercial harm; whether it is depends on how the benefit is presented internally and how the consequences of opening are perceived.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is a lot of stuff behind closed doors that could potentially be open sourced
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Where a specification forces a large FPGA with hard processor cores there are effectively two vendors, and the accompanying toolchain comes with them; nobody rewrites a toolchain against a deadline, so open flows remain unavailable at that end of the market regardless of their merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: you aren't going to go and write, you know, try and blow up a tool chain when you have a deadline
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Publishing open FPGA boards is a deliberate strategy for isolating the remaining closed element: once the board, the IP and the software are open, the only proprietary piece left is the toolchain, which makes the obstruction visible instead of diffuse.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you show people it's possible in different areas and you like chip away at this block, you eventually get to the part where it's just the tool chain
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Vendor toolchains bundle free IP cores, so for most teams the economics favour the proprietary flow: building the equivalent from open blocks is roughly twice the work, and the open option only wins where it is already good enough to be used unchanged.
claims.quote_verbatim: building this from scratch is twice the work that just grabbing Silenx IP
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Open RISC-V soft cores such as VexRiscv are compact enough that a multi-core Linux-capable system on chip fits in an FPGA of around 35 000 lookup tables, so an open soft-core path does not require a large device.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm talking about something that has, you know, 35K LUTs or less
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Putting a memory controller in an FPGA rather than using a fixed system-on-chip is what makes Rowhammer research tractable, because the researcher can modify access patterns directly; using that approach on a Kintex-7 board, new vulnerability classes were found in memories advertised as Rowhammer-protected.
claims.quote_verbatim: being able to tweak your controller means that you can you know fiddle around with what kind of stuff triggers a problem much more easily
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: The argument for open-sourcing a block whose single use case does not justify custom development is aggregation: reuse across unrelated fields is what repays the work, and the same open RTL developed on an FPGA can subsequently be taped out into a real chip unchanged.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can aggregate use cases across different fields and show that there's reuse going on all the time
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A LoRaWAN sensor node was published as a full open release, hardware design files, schematics, PCB, BOM and SDK together, with the explicit intent that it serve as a reference design from which users derive application-specific nodes.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the hardware design files, schematics, PCB, BOM files, and including the SDK, we made it open source
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Generic Nodes with Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: That node used an STM32WL, which carries a Semtech radio design licensed onto ST's die and tested as one part, in a dual-core Cortex-M4 and M0+ variant, with 100 mil headers for programming and expansion, an I2C quick connector, and a 2 V to 5.5 V input range accepting lithium cells or two or three alkaline cells in series.
claims.quote_verbatim: a wide input voltage from two volts up to 5.5 volts with the JST connectors
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Generic Nodes with Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: Choosing an unusual processor for an open project suppresses outside contribution: the JTAGulator was built on a Propeller microcontroller, and its designer attributed the low rate of community contributions to that choice rather than to the project itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes I regret using that compared to like a more standard type of device because I think I'd have more community contributions if it wasn't such an arcane kind of thing
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Non-disclosure agreements are the concrete barrier that open PDKs remove: a training course cannot function if every participant must sign an NDA before touching the tools, so an open process kit is what makes chip design teachable at scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have to make everybody on the training course sign an NDA before they can even start using the tools, that's, that's not, that's not a great start
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: What laboratory instrument buyers pay for is validation for a specific scenario rather than circuit complexity, reinforced by the instrument having appeared in published papers; an open equivalent must supply that validation evidence, not merely the same electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not the most complex gear, but it's the tested for the scenario that they, that they need. And that is worth paying for
claims.speaker: Amitabh Shrivastava
claims.episode_title: Refrigerators and Robots with Amitabh Shrivastava

claims.claim_text: Early third-party ESP8266 development ran on a virtual machine leaked from an Espressif partner that contained the compiler toolchain; the vendor chose to embrace the resulting outside work rather than issue takedowns, and later parts were released with usable tooling from the start.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the early ESP 8266 development was done on this, like leaked VM from some partner customer of Espressif
claims.speaker: Charles Lohr
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: The commercial outcome for a wireless microcontroller vendor turned on tooling access rather than silicon: comparable parts existed, but only one gave outsiders a documented way to run their own code on it, and that access rather than any silicon advantage is what produced the difference.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not because they, it's not because they had some magic Silicon
claims.speaker: Charles Lohr
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Arguments that transplant software practice into hardware understate a scale difference of roughly a thousand to one in community size, so in a given hardware speciality there may be no outside contributor at all; the entry friction is also far higher than pasting a script tag into a page.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the fundamental differences is that the hardware community is one thousandth the size
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Surveyed users of an open real-time operating system gave two reasons for choosing it that are independent of features: guaranteed access to all of the source, and the expectation that they will be able to contribute back, for example by improving documentation. Support for some parts, such as the RP2040, arrived from the community rather than from the maintainers.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the reasons we actually use Zephyr is, is because it's open source. And like, because we know that we're going to have access to all the code
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: A design consultancy can use open-source products as its public portfolio, since client work cannot be shown; the open work doubles as demonstrable capability and as a revenue line from selling the resulting modules.
claims.quote_verbatim: we are also doing our own open-source projects. We have, I would say, a passion for open-source projects. And now we're also making products out of that
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Refusing venture funding is a live option for an open hardware product: the designer of an open pick-and-place machine turned down an investor rather than take the product closed source, having reached a cost base low enough to work full time on modest crowdfunded income.
claims.quote_verbatim: I told him to pound sand because I was not interested in like making it go close source
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: The durable business model for open source hardware is compiling it: software compiles for nothing, whereas turning published files into a working machine costs money and time, so selling the built article is where the value sits.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's effectively free to compile software. It's very expensive and time consuming to quote unquote compile hardware from source
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: The exposure a design faces from being published depends on its niche: a tool bought for production work is bought by people whose time is committed elsewhere, so publishing the files costs few sales, whereas a hobby product sold to people with time to build is more exposed.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're buying a pick in place, chances are you're using it for work, you know? And if you're using it for work, chances are you don't want to build one
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Maintaining open footprints together with Blender models for every component used lets one library serve schematic capture and layout in KiCad, photorealistic visualisation, and thermal and EMC simulation, all with open tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: for all of those components, we have open source footprints and blender models
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Caliptra is a shared open root of trust built around a RISC-V core and developed jointly by companies that compete elsewhere, on the reasoning that a hundred suppliers each shipping a different security block cannot be certified across the cloud providers that must accept them; a single implementation can be certified once and reused.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're not going to have 100 suppliers, you know, develop 100 different security solutions to be tested across like a number of cloud solution providers
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Hardware has plenty of standards but very few open implementations of them, so each vendor implements the standard separately and every implementation must then be certified; supplying a reference implementation alongside the standard is what removes that duplication.
claims.quote_verbatim: But very few open implementations of standards
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: The security argument for an open root-of-trust chip is attestation: if the design is public, a party can in principle verify that the silicon is running the design it claims to run, which answers the question of whether a server operator has been compelled to tamper with its own hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's an open source chip, then you can in theory do, you know, attestation that the design is what's running
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: When one open-silicon shuttle service collapsed, its proprietary internal work would have been lost with it, while the open flow survived and was picked up elsewhere; three routes to open silicon subsequently existed, including IHP in Europe on a 130 nm process, a service in Singapore and a group working with SkyWater.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything eFabulous had done was proprietary. It would have all died when an investors had disagreements
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Having several independent services running the same open flow supplies geographic choice and competitive pressure: a design can be routed to a fab in the required jurisdiction, and a service handling something badly can be bypassed rather than tolerated.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you need your chips manufactured, say in Europe, you now have an option
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A university tympanometry screening device was developed as an open project with all designs published, firmware in Zephyr and a four-layer board captured in KiCad; the design constraints were driven by cost and by removing the need for a trained audiologist to interpret the result.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've open sourced all the designs. The firmware is all written in Zephyr
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Moving an open medical device out of the academic setting requires reconciling commercialisation with the intent to give the design away, and the same safety, quality and regulatory obligations apply as to any commercial device regardless of the licence.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're trying to do this balance of commercializing something we want to give away for free. And it turns out that is an uphill battle
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: An open quadruped robot built around 3D-printed structure and brushless actuators reached a build cost of thirteen hundred dollars, a two thousand dollar reduction on the previous version of the same design, with documentation and video released alongside.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's only $1,300 to build, which is a $2,000 reduction from, from Kara 1.0
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa
claims.episode_title: Robots Everywhere with Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: The first step on a project in an unfamiliar domain is a survey of what has already been published, including failed attempts, since a documented failure tells you what to avoid and convergence across projects reveals the parameter ranges, such as motor speed and torque, that the application actually needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if someone's project like failed, you know why it failed and you can avoid doing whatever they did
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa
claims.episode_title: Robots Everywhere with Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: The users who realise concrete value from open hardware are professional ones: having the design details lets a company take control of its supply chain and continue a product independently of the board vendor, whereas most individual users never need the files.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have that opportunity to kind of take control over the supply chain
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Calling a published design a reference design invites the claim that it was validated for some purpose and creates liability exposure; the defensible position is to state that the design is not validated for any purpose whatsoever and to supply the documentation so the user can validate it themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you, if you, if you directly call it a reference design, it gives them some opportunity to say that, well, this design was validated for some purpose
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Arduino was licensed with the intent that others could build on the work before the term open source hardware existed, so the licence choice preceded and was independent of the definition later formalised by the movement.
claims.quote_verbatim: we wanted to apply like a license to hardware that would encourage people to kind of, I don't know, we wanted them to be able to build upon the work that we did
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The Arduino development environment was derived from Processing, a language and environment built at MIT for designers and artists, with Java replaced by C++; the board and toolchain were also manufactured locally in Ivrea, Italy, where the surrounding electronics industry made short-run PCB fabrication and assembly reachable by car.
claims.quote_verbatim: which is basically was their development environment with Java removed and plugged with C++
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

attribution_notes: Ep 41: the bundle labels the counterfeit-kit support window Dave Jones, but the account of a designer forced to support kits she did not sell belongs to the guest, Jeff Keyzer, and is attributed to him by content. The separate observation that suing over a small kit is not viable is a fused window with no unambiguous owner, so speaker is null.

Ep 43: the bundle's speaker label for this window is the string 'Arduino', which is not a person; the window is a two-guest interview and the trademark explanation cannot be assigned between Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum, so speaker is null.

Ep 87: attribution_reliable is true but the window fuses host and guest. The statement about changing the licence in order to place devices in schools is Ian Daniher speaking about his own company, Nonolith, and is attributed to him by content; the bundle label Dave Jones was overridden.
Ep 113: the bundle labels this window SPEAKER_01. The passage is a multi-party interview and the funding-scale explanation cannot be assigned unambiguously, so speaker is null.

Ep 125: the bundle labels every window SPEAKER_00. The content is unambiguously Ian Lesnet speaking about Dangerous Prototypes, the Bus Pirate, his licensing history and his arrangement with Seeed Studio, so all claims from this episode are attributed to him.
Ep 158: the bundle labels these windows SPEAKER_01. Neither the IBM PC bus history nor the software-defined radio figures can be assigned to a named speaker from the content, so speaker is null.
Ep 163: the bundle labels this window SPEAKER_03. It is a two-founder Upverter interview and the speaker cannot be separated between them, so speaker is null.

Ep 208: the bundle labels the venture-funding-removes-founder-control window Nadya Peek, but that argument is the host Dave Jones responding to her; attributed to him by content. The Fab Lab replication and extensibility claims are Nadya Peek's and keep the bundle label.

Ep 316: the bundle labels the gear-logo and multimeter-manufacturer windows Chris Gammell, but both are Dave Jones setting out his own logo-letters proposal and his own negotiation with a multimeter manufacturer; attributed to him by content. Conversely the practice of using the gear logo only on the fully open board is Robert Feranec describing his own product line, and the bundle's host label was overridden.
Ep 637: the bundle labels this window Chris Gammell, but the Espressif history is the guest, Charles Lohr (CNLohr); attributed to him by content.

Ep 181, 250, 346, 374, 438, 458, 519, 527, 575, 650, 703: attribution_reliable is false, but each window is a single-guest interview in which the quoted technical or historical explanation is unambiguously that named guest (Dave Vandenbout, Vic Aprea, Joe FitzPatrick, Claire Wolf, Bart Dring, Ken Burns, Michael Gielda, Matt Liberty, Joe Grand, Andreas Olofsson, Tim Ansell). Bundle labels retained.
Ep 384: the two windows from this episode were dropped; they concern only the naming of a contest category and carry no transferable content.
One bundle passage has a null episode and was dropped as uncitable.
name: Open Source Hardware
